Pool Leak Detection in Sarasota, FL

Is your pool losing more water than the Florida sun can explain? SRQ Leak Pros connects you with a local pro who tests the shell, fittings and buried pool plumbing to find the leak.

Call (941) 393-1012
  • Sarasota & Manatee counties
  • Service lines, slabs, sewers & pools
  • Homes, condos & businesses
  • Independent local providers

Quick answer: Pool leak detection in Sarasota finds out whether your pool is losing water to a leak or to evaporation, then pinpoints where. A pro starts with a bucket test, dye-tests the shell, lights, skimmer and returns, and pressure-tests the buried lines. Acoustic tools then find the exact spot underground.

Every outdoor pool in Sarasota loses some water to sun, wind and splashing. A leak is different. It drains water steadily, even when no one swims, and it can wash out soil under the deck or the pool itself. The first job is to prove which one you have. The second is to find the leak without breaking up the deck on a guess.

Signs your pool may be leaking

SignWhat it may point to
Pool drops more than a bucket of pool water set on the stepMore loss than evaporation alone
Level drops faster with the pump runningA leak on the pressure side, such as a return line
Level drops faster with the pump offA leak in the shell, light or suction side
Level stops at the skimmer or a lightA leak at that fitting
Wet soil, soft spots or cracks in the deckA buried line leaking
Air in the pump basket or filterA suction-side leak pulling in air
Higher water bill from refillingOngoing water loss

What pool leak detection includes

  • A bucket test to compare pool loss with evaporation
  • Pump-on and pump-off level comparisons
  • Dye testing at the skimmer, returns, main drain, lights and steps
  • A visual check of the pool shell, tile line and coping
  • Pressure testing of each buried pool line
  • Acoustic listening along leaking lines
  • A check of the equipment pad, pump, filter and valves
  • A written report with leak locations and repair options

The bucket test you can do first

The bucket test separates evaporation from a leak.

  1. Fill a bucket with pool water and set it on a pool step so it sits in the water.
  2. Mark the water level inside the bucket and on the pool wall or skimmer.
  3. Leave the pump in its normal setting and wait one full day.
  4. Compare. If the pool dropped more than the bucket, you likely have a leak.
  5. Repeat with the pump off to see which side of the system is leaking.

How a pro finds a pool leak, step by step

  1. Confirm the loss. The pro checks your bucket test or runs a new one.
  2. Inspect the equipment. Pumps, filters, heaters and valves can leak on the pad.
  3. Dye test fittings. A few drops of dye near each fitting show whether water is being pulled out.
  4. Check the shell. Cracks, loose tile and torn liners are inspected, sometimes underwater.
  5. Pressure test the lines. Each line is plugged and pressurized. A line that won't hold pressure is leaking.
  6. Pinpoint underground. A ground microphone or tracer gas finds the exact spot in a leaking line.
  7. Report. You get a list of every leak found and the repair options.

Where pool leaks hide

  • Skimmer. The joint where the skimmer meets the pool shell is a common leak point.
  • Return lines and fittings. The pipes that carry filtered water back into the pool.
  • Main drain. Leaks at the drain fitting or its buried pipe.
  • Lights. The conduit and the light niche can let water escape.
  • Shell cracks. Settling, ground movement or age can crack plaster or concrete.
  • Equipment. A worn pump seal or a cracked valve on the pad.

What affects the cost

No price is listed, because it depends on the pool and what is found. These factors matter:

  • Pool size and type: concrete, fiberglass or vinyl
  • Number of lines and fittings to test
  • Whether a dive inspection is needed
  • Spa and water features attached to the system
  • Repairs needed, which are priced separately

DIY checks vs. calling a pro

Run the bucket test and look for wet spots around the equipment and deck. Check the pump basket for air. Call a pro when the bucket test shows a leak, the deck is cracking or sinking, or you can't find the source. Don't break the deck to look for a buried line. Pressure testing and acoustic tools can narrow the spot first.

Florida notes

Florida law places swimming pool piping within the plumbing contractor's scope, and Florida also issues licenses to pool contractors. Ask the provider which license covers the repair and check it on the DBPR license search. Some homeowners policies may cover sudden damage, but not the cost to find a slow pool leak or repair worn parts. Ask your agent.

Local note

Local note: many pools in Lakewood Ranch and Osprey have long runs from the pool to the equipment pad, which means more buried pipe to test. Seasonal homes on Siesta Key can lose a lot of water before anyone notices.

Pool Leak Detection questions

How much water loss is normal for a pool?

Evaporation varies with sun, wind and humidity. A bucket test is the best way to tell normal loss from a leak in your own pool.

Can a pool leak damage my home or yard?

Yes. A buried line leak can wash out soil under the deck, and a large leak can affect nearby structures. Find it early.

Do I need to drain the pool for leak detection?

Usually not. Most testing is done with the pool full, using dye, pressure tests and listening tools.

Can a pool leak raise my water bill?

Yes. Refilling a leaking pool adds to your water use. A sudden jump in usage with a pool on the property is worth checking.

How long does pool leak detection take?

Many inspections take a few hours. Pools with spas, water features or many lines can take longer.
